title: The Second Naval Battle of Guadalcanal, 14–15 November 1942

clock.name: zone −11 (Guadalcanal)

others.name: US zone −12 (Washington’s and South Dakota’s reports, the war damage report, ONI Part III, Lundgren)

clock.note: Zone −11 (UTC+11), as Morison V, ONI Part I and the TROMs keep it; one official narrative is on two clocks (ONI Part I zone −11, Part III zone −12), and every beat from a zone −12 source carries its own reading. The battle crosses midnight: times after it are written 24:00 and on (R5 §2.1).

cloud.note: thin cloud at 10,000 ft with some low cloud at 2,000 ft (South Dakota) or cirro-cumulus (ONI); overcast by about 01:00

phases.note: after moonset only very prominent landmarks were visible beyond five miles; Washington’s report has visibility falling from nine to three miles

moon.note: computed (R5 §2.1): 11.6° high in the west-south-west at 23:00, setting between 23:50 and 23:58; behind Cape Esperance’s hills about 22:52

weather.note: A calm sea and a light breeze from the south-south-east; warm.

japan.name: Imperial Japanese Navy: the Emergency Bombardment Force of Vice Admiral KONDŌ Nobutake 近藤信竹

events.text: TF 64 stops zigzagging; flashes over the horizon to the west, where Tanaka’s transports are burning.
TF 64 turns west, south of Savo; the moon sets behind the hills of Cape Esperance.
Washington’s radar finds ships to the north-north-west, nine miles off.

tellings.says: SG and fire-control radar contact bearing 340°, 18,000 yards, then 19,600 (0001 zone −12).
“Target distant nine miles, a point and a half west of north.”

events.text: Rear Admiral Willis A. Lee: “You may open fire when you are ready.”
Washington opens fire by radar on the leading ship to the north.

tellings.says: 42 rounds of 16-inch in about three minutes at 18,500 yards; Sendai was not damaged (from her report).

events.text: Washington ceases fire: the target is lost.
TF 64 turns to the west-north-west and works up speed.
Washington’s secondary battery fires on flashes along Savo’s shore.

tellings.says: Fired on “shore batteries” on Savo: Ayanami and the Nagara group.

events.text: Washington’s secondary ceases fire; she comes round to the west at full speed.
Washington’s radar: ships to the north-north-west, hidden by Savo until now.

tellings.says: Four ships bearing 330°.

events.text: Washington passes the burning destroyers.
The moon has set; only the largest landmarks show beyond a few miles.
Washington opens fire on the battleship in the searchlights’ glare, unseen herself.

tellings.says: Bearing 008°, 8,400 yards, main battery and mounts 1 and 3; mounts 5 and 7 on the illuminating ship at 7,500 yards (0100 zone −12).

events.text: Washington’s star shell, from her after mount.

tellings.says: 62 star shells from mount 9 after the second salvo; they fell short and blinded the main-battery spotters.

events.text: Washington checks fire on a false report that her target has sunk.
Lee: “If you can see anything to shoot at, go ahead.” Washington resumes.
Washington ceases fire; her target is burning and turning away.

tellings.says: 117 of a possible 131 sixteen-inch rounds in the night, about 1.55 rounds per gun per minute; 75 at Kirishima and 107 of 5-inch at the battleship.

events.text: Washington turns north after the retreating ships.
Lee reverses course to stay out of a torpedo trap.
Torpedoes run in Washington’s wake and explode astern.

tellings.says: “Seventeen separate torpedoes were noted ... four or five real ‘fish’” (0148–0219 zone −12).

events.text: Washington retires to the south-west, out of the sound.

events.text: South Dakota’s radar: ships to the north-west.
South Dakota opens fire on the second ship of the column to the north; her first salvo straddles.
South Dakota loses power aft: the shock of her own after turret firing.

tellings.says: Turret III firing astern closed an automatic bus transfer switch, paralleling two out-of-phase switchboards; breakers “locked in” by standing instructions cascaded; power off in all turrets from 0033 to 0036 (zone −12), never lost on Turrets I and II or any 5-inch mount but 6 and 8.

events.text: South Dakota’s power returns; she turns to clear the burning destroyers.
South Dakota’s search radar fails for five minutes.
South Dakota’s after turret, firing astern, sets her floatplanes afire; the next salvo blows them overboard.
South Dakota’s target astern explodes and is lost from the radar.
South Dakota’s radar plot: ships close on her starboard bow; earlier reports had been overlooked.
Searchlights fix South Dakota, in pairs, each pair one above the other.

tellings.says: Two illuminations: the cruiser screen’s at 0048 and Atago’s at 0100 (zone −12).
This is the midnight illumination, logged ten minutes early: South Dakota’s chronology runs ten minutes off Washington’s (n. 58).

events.text: South Dakota is hit for the first time.
events.byNote: her log does not name the shooter; Lundgren reads the cruiser screen

events.where: the superstructure and foremast; a heavy shell on Turret III’s barbette that did not penetrate
events.text: Heavy shells strike South Dakota’s superstructure.

tellings.says: One 14-inch hit among at least 26.
Hits 2, 11, 21, 23 and 26 were 14-inch; only hits 2, 11 and 26 detonated at high order.
Kirishima’s lookouts claimed ten 14-inch hits (Ikeda, via Lundgren).

events.text: Atago’s searchlights fix South Dakota at close range.

events.where: the superstructure, radar and fire control
events.text: Eight-inch shells hit South Dakota’s upperworks again and again.

tellings.says: Seventeen 8-inch hits from Atago and Takao, five 6-inch, one 5-inch, besides Kirishima’s.
At least 26 hits: one 5-inch, six 6-inch, eighteen 8-inch, one 14-inch; the armour never penetrated.
42 large-calibre hits.

events.byNote: the WDR’s six 6-inch hits; the light cruisers carried 14 cm (5.5-inch) guns, and which ship fired them is not named
the WDR’s one 5-inch hit; the shooter is not named

events.text: Hits in the superstructure cut fire-control and interior-communication power for about three minutes.
Every radar in South Dakota but one is out; her radar plot is wrecked.
South Dakota breaks off to the south-west at full speed.
South Dakota’s fires are out.

fate.note: superstructure wrecked, an after turret hard to train, all but one radar out; she retired

tellings.says: 38 men killed or missing and 60 wounded.
Thirty men were killed and 60 wounded.
39 killed, 59 wounded (Frank; verify).

events.where: starboard, frame 45; the forecastle blown off to the bridge
events.text: Walke is torpedoed; her bow is blown away.
events.byNote: whose torpedoes hit Walke is not settled (Lundgren: Nagara’s destroyers or Ayanami)

tellings.says: A torpedo at frame 45 starboard, then a “cruiser salvo”, while she was shifting her torpedoes from curved fire ahead to broadside: her torpedoes never fired.

events.text: Walke sinks.

tellings.says: She sank at 23:36 by his adjusted time; her depth charges exploded under the men in the water a minute later.
Six officers and 76 enlisted men killed or missing (from Walke’s report).
151 were landed at Tulagi, where 6 died of wounds (Walke’s report, n. 76).

tellings.says: An enemy heavy cruiser came in on the port side of the column “virtually undetected”, and part of an 8-inch salvo (probably three shells) hit her; she capsized in half a minute.

Preston sinks.

events.where: aft; the shell does not explode

events.text: Gwin ceases fire: no targets.
Lee orders the destroyers to retire; Gwin is the one fit to steam away.

tellings.says: The hit killed all the personnel on the upper level of No. 2 engine room.

events.text: Kirishima’s bridge sees a battleship lying dark against Guadalcanal: South Dakota.
Kirishima opens fire on South Dakota, secondary guns first.

tellings.says: Her guns were loaded with Type 3 incendiary shells on reduced charges for the airfield; changing to armour-piercing meant firing them out, three to five minutes of continuous fire.

events.text: Kondō’s column turns to the south-east.

events.where: a straddle; the splashes soak the bridge
events.text: Washington’s first salvo straddles Kirishima.

events.where: the pagoda and compass bridge; amidships near the casemates; the bow and the forward turrets
events.text: Kirishima: heavy shells in the bridge and forward; the forward turrets are wrecked.

tellings.says: Between 17 and 21 hits by 16-inch shells and 17 to 20 by 5-inch, from Ikeda’s sketch, Ballard’s 1992 film and the 2019 survey.
About nine 16-inch and about forty 5-inch hits (Tokuno).
“9 out of 75.”
“About eight.”
Lee’s report: eight 16-inch (note 5).
17 to 20 five-inch hits; Tokuno’s 40 would be 37 per cent of 107 rounds, “simply too high”.

events.where: the stern and the after hydraulic pump room; below the waterline
events.text: Kirishima: hits aft and below the waterline.
Kirishima: rudders jammed; she begins to circle to port.

tellings.says: Rudders jammed at 10 degrees starboard.
The wreck shows the starboard rudder about 12° to starboard and the port rudder about 85°, which pulls her to port.

events.text: Kirishima: fires fore and aft.
Kirishima steadies westward, still making way.
Kirishima’s fires are coming under control.

tellings.says: “By 0249” most fires are put out: an hour from Lundgren’s time.

events.text: Kirishima: her steering compartment floods; divers cannot reach it.
Kirishima lists one way and the other as her voids are counter-flooded; Nagara refuses a tow and the destroyers try and fail.
Her magazines flooded, Kirishima is abandoned, Asagumo alongside to starboard and Teruzuki to port.
events.note: in the small hours; no closer time in what was read

events.text: Kirishima capsizes to port and sinks.

tellings.says: Capsized at 0325 at 09°05′S 159°42′E.
“0323” in an essay otherwise on zone −12, which would be 02:23 here; she capsized to port while being abandoned, not scuttled.
The captain ordered the Kingston valves opened, “about two and one-half hours” after the first hit.
212 lost their lives; Captain IWABUCHI Sanji 岩淵三次, Ono and 1,098 were rescued.
About 209 killed; 61 officers and petty officers and 1,031 sailors rescued.
About 250 of about 1,400.

stops.text: 20:10, zone −11. Rear Admiral Willis A. Lee’s TF 64 comes up from the south-west to sweep round Savo: the destroyers ahead, Washington and South Dakota astern. Far to the west the transports of Rear Admiral TANAKA Raizō 田中頼三, bombed all day, are burning.

21:48. North of Savo, TF 64 turns down the island’s eastern side. Japanese voices are heard on the radio; PT boats at Tulagi take the battleships for the enemy until Lee answers them in plain language.
22:52. South of Savo the column turns west. The moon is setting behind the hills of Cape Esperance; within the hour only the largest landmarks will show beyond a few miles.
23:16. Washington’s radar has had ships to the north for a quarter of an hour. She opens fire by radar; Sendai turns away behind smoke and is not hit.
23:30. From Savo’s shadow Ayanami and Nagara’s destroyers loose their torpedoes. Within minutes Preston rolls over, Walke and Benham are torpedoed, and Gwin is hit in an engine room.

23:33. South Dakota’s power fails aft: the shock of her own after turret firing has cascaded through her switchboards. For three minutes her turrets are dead; then she turns to clear the burning destroyers and shows herself against them.
23:51. From Kirishima’s bridge a battleship is seen, dark against the mass of Guadalcanal. Kirishima opens fire. Searchlights from the Japanese screen have already found South Dakota.
00:00. Atago’s searchlights fix South Dakota at close range, and the Japanese fire falls on her. Washington, unlit and unseen, now knows which ship is her sister: she opens on Kirishima by radar.

00:07. Washington ceases fire. Kirishima is burning fore and aft, her forward turrets wrecked and her rudders jammed; she circles to port. South Dakota, her upperworks shot through, breaks off to the south-west.
00:33. Rear Admiral Willis A. Lee turns his flagship back to the south to keep out of a torpedo trap. Torpedoes chase Washington and burst in her wake; none hits.
03:20. Her magazines flooded and her steering compartment awash, Kirishima capsizes to port north-west of Savo while her crew are leaving her.

objective.text: Hold fire until you are sure which ship is South Dakota. Then hit the battleship in the searchlights.

after.text: Washington held her fire until the Japanese searchlights showed which ship was South Dakota. Then she fired by radar into Kirishima, unlit and unseen herself. Within minutes Kirishima’s forward turrets were out, fires were burning fore and aft and her rudders were jammed; she circled to port and could not be steered again. Her crew flooded her magazines and began to leave her; she capsized north-west of Savo in the small hours. Washington was not hit. How many of her shells struck is still argued.

tellings.says: Rear Admiral Willis A. Lee’s report: eight 16-inch hits; 212 of Kirishima’s crew lost their lives.

after.text: Kirishima found South Dakota against the dark of the land and hit her, as the cruisers did. The second battleship was never seen from Kirishima’s bridge: the glare of the searchlights hid her. Within minutes the forward turrets were wrecked and hits aft had jammed the rudders. Kirishima circled and could not be steered. She was abandoned, and capsized to port with men still aboard.

tellings.says: “We couldn’t see it because of the glare from the destroyers’ searchlights”: TOKUNO Horishi, Kirishima’s assistant gunnery officer, of Washington.

after.text: Gwin lit the targets with star shell, then fired on the destroyer shooting along Savo’s shore and hit her. She was hit in an engine room as Preston rolled over ahead of her, and the shock dropped torpedoes over the side. She was the only one of the van destroyers fit to steam away; the next day she sank the crippled Benham.

tellings.says: Walke: six officers and 76 enlisted men killed or missing.
Preston: 131 picked up by Meade; Benham abandoned without loss of life.

objective.text: Close the American column under the island’s shadow and fire your torpedoes before your guns.

checkpoints.text: The American van is broken; the battleships are coming on behind it.

record.note: whose torpedoes hit Walke and Benham is not settled; Lundgren gives Benham’s to Nagara’s destroyers and suggests Preston’s capsizing may be Ayanami’s

after.text: Ayanami came round Savo alone and fired her torpedoes before her guns, as doctrine taught. Minutes later the American destroyers were torpedoed, by her spread or Nagara’s. Then the American column found her against the island; she stopped, burning, and was scuttled after her crew had gone across to Uranami.

tellings.says: Her captain claimed one cruiser and one destroyer sunk and a third destroyer on fire.
The whole Naval Battle of Guadalcanal, 12–15 November: US 1,732 killed; Japanese 1,900, transports excluded (Frank and Lundstrom; verify).
